section_summary: This section surveys Japan’s early post-surrender political reorganization, including proposed purges, party maneuvering, Communist and Socialist activity, Soviet press criticism, constitutional reform, and the October 1945 imperial amnesty. It also contains Prince Fumimaro Konoe’s recollections of the breakdown of Japanese-American negotiations in 1941, together with memoranda of his conversations about the road to war. A separate report describes administrative, military, and economic conditions in recently transferred Formosa.

subfiles.title: Continuation of report advocating a purge of wartime politicians and bureaucrats
subfiles.about: The concluding page argues that democratic reform requires the removal of politicians and bureaucrats associated with wartime militarism.
subfiles.summary: Continuation of a report listing politicians collaborating with the Tojo Cabinet and bureaucratic cliques in three ministries, urging a thorough purge.

subfiles.title: Charge-out record for State Department file item
subfiles.about: A records-control sheet documents the charging out of an item identified as A-139 from Baghdad.
subfiles.summary: Charge-out record for file 867N.6363/4-2648 (A-139 from Baghdad); a later archival sheet, not part of the 1945 file.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 92 forwarding weekly report on Japanese political parties
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Acting United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Atcheson forwards the mission’s report on Japanese political-party developments during the week ending December 8, 1945.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 92 encloses the latest weekly survey of the Progressive, Liberal, Social Democratic and Communist parties.

subfiles.title: Political Parties in Japan: Developments During the Week Ending December 8, 1945
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.to: George Atcheson Jr. / Department of State
subfiles.about: A detailed weekly survey analyzes Japanese parties, leadership disputes, electoral plans, and reactions to arrests for war crimes.
subfiles.summary: The Progressive Party faced possible fragmentation after Ota Masataka and Kaya Okinori were identified as war-crimes suspects, while General Ugaki and several civilian elder statesmen were considered for its presidency. Liberal leader Ando Masazumi described his party’s free-market program and support for electoral, labor, and land reforms, while defending retention of the Emperor. The report maps the right, center, and left factions of the Social Democratic Party and its rejection of Communist united-front proposals. It also describes the Communist Party’s fourth congress, membership, officers, finances, anti-imperial propaganda, youth program, and mass meetings naming alleged war criminals.

subfiles.title: Request for declassification of Despatch No. 92
subfiles.from: Wilson C. Flake, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The form requests and authorizes declassification of Atcheson’s December 11, 1945 despatch.
subfiles.summary: Declassification of Despatch No. 92, from confidential to unclassified, authorized February 1, 1952.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 99 transmitting conversations with Prince Konoe
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Acting United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Atcheson forwards two memoranda of Bishop’s November 1945 conversations with former prime minister Prince Konoe.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 99 summarizes Konoe's account of missed 1937 mediation, 1941 diplomacy versus military preparation, Tojo's ultimatum view and the proposed Roosevelt meeting.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Prince Konoe, November 6, 1945
subfiles.from: Max W. Bishop, Office of the United States Political Adviser
subfiles.to: Office of the United States Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Konoe discusses Japanese diplomacy from the 1937 China Incident through the American note of November 26, 1941.
subfiles.summary: Konoe, November 6, 1945: Hirota did not tell him of 1937 mediation offers; 1941 was a race between diplomacy and deployments; the Privy Council did not unanimously accept the ultimatum view.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Prince Konoe, November 7, 1945
subfiles.from: Max W. Bishop, Office of the United States Political Adviser
subfiles.to: Office of the United States Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Konoe recounts the policy struggle that led to his October 1941 resignation and Tojo’s appointment as prime minister.
subfiles.summary: Konoe, November 7, 1945: the September 6 war-preparation decision, his clash with Tojo over China withdrawal, Navy doubts, and a Roosevelt meeting he thought might yield an imperial withdrawal order.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 961 forwarding a report on conditions in Formosa
subfiles.from: Charge d’Affaires ad interim, U.S. Embassy, Chongqing
subfiles.about: The embassy forwards Military Attaché for Air Otto R. Haney’s observations from a five-day visit to Formosa.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 961 encloses Haney's December 12 memorandum on post-surrender Formosa conditions.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on conditions in Formosa
subfiles.from: Lieutenant Colonel Otto R. Haney, U.S. Military Attaché for Air, Chongqing
subfiles.about: Haney reports on civil administration, Japanese disarmament, transport, economic conditions, utilities, and an American presence in Formosa.
subfiles.summary: Haney: Governor-General Chen Yi able but understaffed; 170,000 Japanese troops awaiting repatriation, growing resentment of Chinese rule, and he recommends an American representative on the island.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-41 transmitting biographical information
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo, for George Atcheson Jr.
subfiles.about: The Department sends biographical information on four Japanese public figures.
subfiles.summary: Airgram A-41 lists biographical information on Hatoyama, Kagawa, Kawai and another, for Atcheson as acting political adviser.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 4222 on Soviet press treatment of Japan
subfiles.about: The telegram summarizes Soviet press criticism of Japanese political developments and the preservation of the Emperor system.
subfiles.summary: Moscow reports TASS on Diet election focus and Ono on Socialist-Communist cooperation, and an Izvestia article arguing militarists cannot be self-reformed into democrats.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 220 on Konoe’s constitutional reform plan
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The telegram relays a press account of Konoe’s proposed constitutional restrictions on imperial authority.
subfiles.summary: Konoe's plan retains the emperor as sovereign, adds mechanisms for the Diet and ordinances, makes military command a state matter, and criticizes independent supreme command and direct appeals to the throne.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 182 forwarding a memorandum on the Japanese amnesty
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Atcheson answers Charles B. Fahs’s request for information about the imperial amnesty of October 17, 1945.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 182 forwards a staff memorandum on the legal basis, scope and political significance of the Japanese amnesty.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Japanese Amnesty of October 17, 1945
subfiles.from: Robert A. Fearey, staff of the United States Political Adviser
subfiles.about: The memorandum explains the legal history, categories, and effects of Japan’s October 1945 imperial amnesty.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum on the October 17, 1945 amnesty: nearly a million offenders, about 320,000 pardoned, 37,000 commuted, 600,000 civil rights restored. Few released political prisoners besides Communists were politically active.

subfiles.title: Duplicate covering despatch for Despatch No. 182
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: A second copy repeats the covering letter transmitting the Japanese-amnesty memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate cover despatch for Despatch No. 182, citing Fahs's request and the October 17, 1945 amnesty memorandum.

subfiles.title: The Memoirs of Prince Fumimaro Konoe, translated from the Asahi Shimbun
subfiles.from: Prince Fumimaro Konoe; translated from the Asahi Shimbun
subfiles.about: Konoe recounts the origins and early course of the secret Japanese-American negotiations conducted by his Cabinet in 1941.
subfiles.summary: Konoe argues that war had to be avoided because Germany’s invasion of the Soviet Union undermined the Tripartite alignment, naval leaders lacked confidence in a long war with the United States, and Japan depended on foreign strategic materials. He describes the Navy’s reluctant acceptance of the Tripartite Pact, competing estimates of petroleum supplies, and the dispute between advocates of negotiation and those who claimed economic strangulation required immediate war. The memoir reproduces an early American negotiating proposal covering China, trade, Pacific security, the Axis alliance, emigration, and a Roosevelt-Konoe meeting at Honolulu, then describes Japanese revisions led by Foreign Minister Matsuoka. It recounts Matsuoka’s unsuccessful neutrality-pact proposal, his consultations with Germany and Italy, the Emperor’s concern, Hull’s suspicions of Japan’s revised terms, and German objections to the negotiations. The excerpt ends mid-account after Ambassador Ott demands explicit Japanese commitments to the Tripartite Pact.
